820.title: Dante (1320)
820.hook: a journey through hell, purgatory and paradise, ending in the love that moves the sun and the other stars
820.carry: the love that moves the sun
820.howItsDone: In Italy the Divine Comedy is read in schools and in public readings, including in churches, and popes, among them Benedict XV and Francis, have written in praise of Dante as a Christian poet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Helfta, and a heartbeat John never wrote about. Your line was the heart of christ.

A man wakes up lost. He's in the middle of his life, in a dark forest, and he can't say how he got there; the straight road is gone. That's how the poem opens, in Italian: nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita, in the middle of the road of our life. The man is the poet himself, Dante Alighieri of Florence, and before he finds his way out he will walk down through hell, climb a mountain, and rise through the heavens.
screen: `LOST IN A DARK WOOD.` → `IN THE MIDDLE OF THE ROAD OF OUR LIFE.` → `DANTE ALIGHIERI OF FLORENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. The poem we call the Divine Comedy comes in three parts. In the Inferno, the Roman poet Virgil leads Dante down through hell, where souls are fixed in the choices they refused to let go of. In the Purgatorio, they climb a mountain where souls are being healed and made ready for God, singing as they go. In the Paradiso, Beatrice, a Florentine woman Dante had loved, guides him up through the heavens. Second, a detail hiding in plain sight. Each part ends on the same word: stars. Hell ends as they climb out to see the stars again. Purgatory ends with Dante pure and ready to rise to the stars. And Paradise ends with l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle, the love that moves the sun and the other stars. Third, that last line. At the very top, Dante is given a glimpse of God, and he says his words fail him. What's left isn't a speech. It's motion: his desire and his will turning, he says, like a wheel moved evenly by that love. Finally, why it fits this path. The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims, "God is charity." Dante's last line reads like that sentence set in motion. In the poem, the love he finds at the end isn't a feeling in him. It's the thing that turns the sun, and at last turns him.
screen: `DOWN, UP, AND THROUGH THE HEAVENS.` · `EVERY PART ENDS ON THE STARS.` · `WORDS FAIL; THE WHEEL TURNS.` · `GOD IS CHARITY.` · then, large: `THE LOVE THAT MOVES THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture the dark first, the way Dante's poem starts, then the first star coming out, and breathe slowly between dark and light. If you pray, hold the line God is charity; if not, hold the poem's last words, the love that moves the sun and the other stars, and let them be a question.

821.title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
821.hook: a third of Europe dies; Jews are scapegoated, and Pope Clement VI condemns the killings
821.howItsDone: The Catholic Church remembers sins committed by Christians against the Jewish people in documents and acts of repentance, such as the Day of Pardon liturgy under Pope John Paul II, and Catholic teaching since the Second Vatican Council rejects blaming Jews collectively.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dante, from a dark wood to the last line of paradise. Your line was the love that moves the sun. Today's story is darker.

A rumor travels faster than the sickness. In town after town along the trade roads, people are dying in their houses, and nobody can say why. Then someone says the wells have been poisoned. Someone else says who did it: the Jews. In some towns, Jewish families who had lived beside their Christian neighbors are driven out, or burned. The sickness keeps coming anyway. Today, that terrible season, told honestly, and one voice that refused the lie.
screen: `A RUMOR FASTER THAN THE SICKNESS.` → `THE WELLS, AND A LIE.` → `ONE VOICE REFUSES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the sickness. A plague swept across Europe. Households were lost, and some towns couldn't bury their dead fast enough. Nobody understood how it spread, and fear went looking for a cause it could see. Second, the blame. In towns along the Rhine and elsewhere, Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells. Mobs, and sometimes town councils, killed many of them. This happened in Christian towns, at the hands of Christians. The Church remembers it, and does not excuse it. Third, the pope. Clement the Sixth, living in Avignon, issued decrees against the killings. His argument rested on plain evidence: Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and it was striking places where no Jews lived at all, so the accusation made no sense. He ordered the clergy to protect Jews, and threatened with excommunication anyone who harmed them. His words did not stop every mob. But they named the lie. Fourth, the Gospel's own refusal. In John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask, in the Douay-Rheims: "who hath sinned, this man, or his parents, that he should be born blind?" Jesus answers: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." He refuses to turn suffering into blame, even with it right in front of him. In a Lenten liturgy of repentance, Pope John Paul the Second asked forgiveness for sins Christians had committed against the Jewish people. Remembering the plague years honestly is part of that.

822.title: Julian of Norwich (c. 1343–after 1416)
822.hook: a woman walled in beside a church sees that all shall be well
822.howItsDone: Catholics read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love in prayer groups and on retreat, and some visit her rebuilt cell at Saint Julian's Church in Norwich; she is honored as Blessed or as a saint in different calendars, though she has not been formally canonized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement, the pope who named the lie behind the killings. Your line was no scapegoats.

Against the wall of a church in Norwich, in England, stands a small room. One window looks into the church, toward the altar, so the woman inside can follow the Mass. Another opens to the outside, so people from the town can come and talk to her. She doesn't come out. She chose this, with the Church's blessing, and she will spend her life here, praying. Her own name isn't certain. History knows her by the name of the church, Saint Julian's.
screen: `A ROOM AGAINST A CHURCH WALL.` → `ONE WINDOW IN, ONE WINDOW OUT.` → `WE KNOW HER AS JULIAN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. An anchoress is a woman who, with the bishop's blessing, is enclosed for life in a cell attached to a church, to give her days to prayer. A man who did the same was called an anchorite. It sounds like a prison, but it was a vocation, asked for and tested, and people from the town could come to the window for counsel. Next, the showings. Julian writes that she once fell so sick that those around her thought she was dying. A priest held a crucifix before her eyes. Then, she says, she was given a series of showings, visions of Christ's passion and of God's love, and she spent years thinking about them and writing them down. The book is called Revelations of Divine Love. Then, the line. Julian lived in the same century as yesterday's plague, and she doesn't look away from sin or pain. She asks, plainly, why God allowed sin at all. The answer she hears, in Grace Warrack's translation, is this: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Finally, what the line is not. It isn't a shrug, and it isn't a promise that nothing bad will happen. Julian hears it in the middle of her question about sin and suffering, and she keeps asking afterward. It's a promise spoken from inside the pain, about where things are going, not a denial of where they are.
screen: `ENCLOSED BESIDE A CHURCH, FOR LIFE.` · `SICK, AND SHOWN A CRUCIFIX.` · `WHY DID GOD ALLOW SIN?` · `A PROMISE FROM INSIDE THE PAIN.` · then, large: `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Let one real worry come to mind, not the biggest, and look at it honestly without pretending it's fine. Then, on each slow out-breath, say Julian's words quietly: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. If you pray, let them be your prayer; if not, notice what it's like to hold a worry and a hope at once.

823.title: The hazelnut
823.hook: Julian is shown all that is made as small as a hazelnut, kept because God loves it
823.howItsDone: Catholics who pray with Julian's Revelations of Divine Love return to the hazelnut passage in retreats and spiritual reading, and some keep a small stone or nut as a reminder of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian the anchoress, in her cell beside the church. Your line was all shall be well. Today, one more of her showings.

Hold out one hand, palm up. Empty. Now set something very small in it in your mind: a bead, a seed, a nut, something you could lose in a coat pocket and never notice. Julian of Norwich says that in one of her showings God put a thing like that in the palm of her hand. Round as a ball, small enough to close her fingers over. And when she asked what it was, an answer came.
screen: `AN EMPTY PALM.` → `SOMETHING ROUND AND SMALL.` → `WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the thing in her hand. In Grace Warrack's translation, Julian says she was shown "a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand." She looked at it with what she calls the eye of her understanding, and wondered what it could be. The answer came: "It is all that is made." Everything, in a shape small enough to hold. Second, her fear. Julian wonders how it can last at all. It's so small, she thinks, it might suddenly fall into nothing. That's an honest worry, and an old one: the world can feel that fragile. Third, the answer. She is told that it lasts, and always will, because God loves it. Not because it's strong, or large, or useful, or earned it. It is kept because it is loved. Fourth, what she sees in it. Julian says she saw three things in this little thing: that God made it, that God loves it, and that God keeps it. Made, loved, kept. She doesn't leave it as a lesson about the universe. She goes straight on to speak of us, and of why we look for rest in things so small. For her, it's the same promise as all shall be well, made small enough to carry.

824.title: Catherine and Avignon
824.hook: the popes live in France for seventy years; a dyer's daughter urges the pope back to Rome
824.howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and Europe; her feast is kept in the spring, and her letters are read for their mix of tenderness and bold counsel to Church leaders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian's hazelnut, all that is made, small in her palm. Your line was kept because loved.

The bishop of Rome, in this story, doesn't live in Rome. He lives in a great palace in Avignon, a city on the Rhône in southern France, and so did the popes before him, one after another, for many years. Rome waits. Then letters start arriving at the papal palace from a young woman in Siena. She isn't a nun in a convent, or a noblewoman, or a scholar. Her father dyes cloth for a living. And she is telling the pope, with great tenderness and no fear at all, to come home.
screen: `THE POPE LIVES IN AVIGNON.` → `ROME WAITS.` → `LETTERS FROM SIENA.`

segments.voice: First, the situation. The popes had settled at Avignon, near the French crown, and stayed through a long run of reigns. To Catherine, and to others in Italy, it looked as if the Church's center had drifted from the city of Peter and Paul. Second, the woman. Catherine of Siena was a laywoman of the Dominican family, wearing its habit while living at home. Tradition says she learned to read later in life, and much of what she sent out, she dictated. Her letters went to popes, kings, queens, even captains of hired soldiers. Third, how she spoke to the pope. She called him, in her Italian, dolce Cristo in terra, sweet Christ on earth. That's not flattery; it's a title of honor and a weight. In her letters to Gregory the Eleventh, she tells him again and again to return to Rome, to be a brave man and not a fearful one, and to trust God more than the voices advising delay. She even traveled to Avignon to tell him in person. Fourth, what happened. Gregory did go back to Rome. Historians weigh many reasons for his choice. Catherine's voice is one the Church remembers, and Catholics now honor her as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and of Europe. Her letters show a way of urging: honor and plain words, sent straight to the one who needed to hear them.

825.title: Catherine's Dialogue
825.hook: her book of conversations with God on truth, love and the bridge that is Christ
825.howItsDone: Catholics read Catherine's Dialogue as spiritual reading, especially on her feast and in Dominican communities, and her image of Christ the bridge appears in retreats and homilies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena and the pope in Avignon. Your line was go back to rome. Today, Catherine again, in conversation with God.

Some books argue. Some books instruct. This one listens and answers. A soul asks God a question, about herself, about the Church, about the whole world, and God replies, at length, and then she asks again. Catherine of Siena dictated this book to friends who wrote it down, and it's known simply as the Dialogue. At its center is a picture she never lets go of: a road broken in two, and something laid across the gap.
screen: `A BOOK THAT ASKS AND ANSWERS.` → `DICTATED, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `A ROAD BROKEN IN TWO.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. The Dialogue is built as a conversation. Catherine brings petitions to God, for herself, for the Church, for the world, and God answers, teaching her through each one. It's a book of prayer with two voices, not a lecture. Second, the broken road. In the Dialogue, God tells Catherine that sin broke the road between heaven and earth, so that no one could cross by their own strength. A river of trouble ran below. Third, the bridge. So, God says, I made my Son a bridge. It reaches from heaven to earth because in Christ God's nature is joined to ours. And it has three steps, which she links to his body on the cross: the nailed feet, the opened side, and the mouth. At the feet the soul first climbs, out of fear; the side shows the heart, where it learns love; at the mouth it finds peace. Catherine ties all this to Jesus's words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Fourth, the cell. Catherine also speaks of a cell of self-knowledge, an inner room where the soul comes to know itself honestly, and inside it, knows God's goodness. Truth about yourself and love from God, together, so that neither turns to despair or pride. That's the Dialogue in small: questions brought honestly, and a bridge that, in Catherine's telling, the soul climbs step by step.
screen: `A CONVERSATION, NOT A LECTURE.` · `THE ROAD WAS BROKEN.` · `FEET, SIDE, MOUTH.` · `THE CELL OF SELF-KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `CHRIST IS THE BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: Bring one real question, not a polished one, about your life, someone you love, or the world. If you pray, say it to God plainly, then stop and wait, as if an answer might come back, and ask again if you need to; if you don't, put it to the quiet and listen to what rises. Either way, let it be a conversation rather than a speech.

826.title: The Western Schism (1378–1417)
826.hook: rival popes, divided saints, forty confusing years
826.howItsDone: Catholics today recognize the Roman line of popes from the schism years as the legitimate one, while honoring saints from both sides, and they pray for Christian unity, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine's Dialogue, a conversation with God about a broken road. Your line was christ is the bridge. Today closes the week.

The pope is finally back in Rome. Catherine's letters, the long wait, the journey home: it's done. Then the pope dies, and the cardinals meet to choose the next one, with crowds in the streets outside shouting for a Roman, or at least an Italian. They elect a man who takes the name Urban the Sixth. Later, some of those same cardinals leave Rome, say the election was forced by the crowd, and choose someone else, who settles in Avignon. Now there are rival popes, each with his own cardinals, each sure he is the true successor of Peter.
screen: `BACK IN ROME, AT LAST.` → `A FRIGHTENED ELECTION.` → `RIVAL POPES.`

segments.voice: First, the split. A schism is a tear in the Church's unity, and this one ran right through the West. Kingdoms took sides. Some dioceses ended up with rival bishops. Ordinary Catholics, trying to be faithful, couldn't easily tell which pope was the real one, and honest people chose differently. Second, the saints. Catherine of Siena backed Urban in Rome with all her energy. Vincent Ferrer, a Dominican preacher later honored as a saint too, backed the Avignon line for years. Holy, prayerful people stood on opposite sides of the question. The facts were truly tangled, and Catholics today honor saints from both sides. Third, the attempted cure. A council met at Pisa to end the split, deposed the rival popes, and elected a new one. But the others refused to step down, and now there was one more claimant than before. Fourth, the end. Another council, at Constance, finally untangled it: one claimant resigned, the others were set aside, and a single pope, Martin the Fifth, was elected and accepted. Through all of it, Christians could pray Jesus's words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one." It's a prayer for unity, prayed by him, and it held even when Christians couldn't agree whom to follow.
screen: `ONE CHURCH, RIVAL POPES.` · `SAINTS ON BOTH SIDES.` · `A CURE THAT ADDS A CLAIMANT.` · `A COUNCIL AT CONSTANCE ENDS IT.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you honestly can't figure out right now, a decision or a question where good people see it differently, and hold it without forcing an answer. If you pray, hold Jesus's words, that they all may be one, and ask for light; if not, let the confusion be there without fighting it, and breathe.
Western Schism. The years when rival popes divided the Western Church and saints stood on both sides, until a council at Constance healed the split. Today's word.
